title: Implement Stack using Queues
description: Brute force to optimized: two queues rebuilt on every push versus a single queue rotated in place to keep the newest element at the front.

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Implement a Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) stack using only the standard operations of a queue (push to the back, pop from the front, peek the front, and check if empty). The implemented stack should support push, pop (removing and returning the top element), top (returning the top element without removing it), and empty.

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Implement X using only Y's primitive operations\"","Simulate the target structure's behavior by cleverly rearranging elements using only the allowed primitive's operations"],["LIFO (stack) needed, FIFO (queue) provided","Rotate the queue after each push so the newest element ends up at the front, mimicking LIFO order"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

A queue naturally returns elements in the order they were inserted (FIFO), while a stack must return the MOST RECENTLY inserted element first (LIFO). The core challenge is making the newest element accessible from the queue's front, which only naturally exposes the OLDEST element.

blocks.title: Analogy: Turning a Line at a Buffet into a Stack of Plates
blocks.text: Picture people queuing for food, always served in arrival order. To make the MOST RECENT arrival get served first instead (like a stack of plates, last one placed is first one taken), each new arrival could cut to the front by having everyone else briefly step behind them, one at a time.

blocks.caption: After pushing, rotating the queue so all older elements move behind the new one makes it act like a stack push

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: push(1), push(2), top(), pop(), empty()
Results: null, null, 2, 2, false. After pushing 1 then 2, top() returns 2 (the most recent), pop() removes and returns 2, and empty() is false since 1 remains.
5. How Should We Think?

Before using two queues to shuffle elements around on every operation, notice that a SINGLE queue suffices if, immediately after pushing a new element to its back, the queue is rotated so that new element moves all the way to the front, at the cost of making push O(n) instead of O(1).

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: A queue naturally exposes its OLDEST element at the front, but a stack needs its NEWEST element accessible instead.

Observation 2: If, right after pushing a new element to the back of the queue, every OTHER element (all the ones pushed before it) is individually dequeued from the front and immediately re-enqueued to the back, the new element ends up at the very front after exactly (queue size - 1) such rotations.

Observation 3: Once this rotation is done after every push, the front of the queue ALWAYS holds the most recently pushed element, so pop() and top() become simple, direct queue-front operations.

Observation 4: This trades an O(1) push (as a queue) for an O(n) push (as a stack), but keeps pop and top at O(1), a valid and common trade-off depending on which operation is more frequent.

This leads to maintaining a single queue, and after every push, rotating it by (current size - 1) positions so the newly pushed element ends up at the front, making pop and top simple front-of-queue operations.
6. Brute Force Solution

Use TWO queues: push new elements into a fresh, empty queue, then move all existing elements from the old queue into the new one, making the new one's front hold the just-pushed element. Swap the two queues afterward.
Step by step algorithm

items: To push x: enqueue x into an initially empty second queue.
Move every element from the original queue into the second queue, one at a time (dequeue from queue1, enqueue into queue2).
Swap the names/roles of queue1 and queue2, so queue1 (the "active" one) now has x at its front.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Using a second queue makes the "new element goes to the front" logic straightforward to reason about.
It requires maintaining and swapping two queue objects, slightly more bookkeeping than necessary.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) per push (moving all existing elements), O(1) for pop, top, empty.
Space: O(n) for the queue(s).

Limitation: this is already an accepted, efficient approach; the single-queue version below achieves the identical time complexity with slightly less bookkeeping, using in-place rotation instead of a second queue.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why a second queue is not strictly necessary: the same "new element ends up at the front" effect can be achieved with just ONE queue, by rotating it in place immediately after the push.

The single-queue rotation trick: after pushing x to the back of the (only) queue, dequeue and immediately re-enqueue every element that was in the queue BEFORE x (there are exactly size-1 of them), which cycles x around to the front.

Why this is equivalent: rotating a queue by moving its front element to its back, repeated (size-1) times, has the same net effect as building a second queue with x first and then appending everyone else, just without the extra queue object.

The core idea: maintain exactly one queue; after every push, rotate it so the new element becomes the front.

Maintain a single queue. On push, enqueue the new value, then dequeue-and-immediately-re-enqueue every one of the OTHER (size-1) elements, cycling the new value to the front. pop, top, and empty operate directly on the front of this single queue.

blocks.caption: A single queue, rotated after every push, keeps the newest element at the front

blocks.text: Why This Works

Rotating the queue by exactly (size - 1) positions right after a push moves every element that existed before the push to the back, in their original relative order, while the just-pushed element ends up at the front. This guarantees the queue's front always holds the most recently pushed element, exactly matching stack (LIFO) semantics, while pop, top, and empty remain simple, direct, O(1) queue-front operations.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) per push (the rotation), O(1) for pop, top, and empty.
Space: O(n) for the single queue.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

Implement Stack using Queues is a foundational "simulate one structure's behavior using another's primitives" problem, showing how a rotation trick can convert FIFO order into LIFO order using a single queue.
Common Mistakes

items: Rotating the wrong number of times (should be exactly size-1, not size), which would leave the new element in the wrong position.
Forgetting that this approach makes push expensive (O(n)) in exchange for cheap pop/top, an intentional and acceptable trade-off here.

blocks.text: Interview Tips

Explicitly stating the push/pop cost trade-off (expensive push, cheap pop, versus the reverse if rotating on pop instead) shows awareness that both variants are valid design choices depending on the expected usage pattern.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "implement X using only Y's operations", think: simulate the missing capability by strategically rearranging elements using only the allowed primitive operations.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would you instead make push O(1) and pop/top O(n) (rotating on pop instead of push)?
How would you implement a queue using only two stacks, the converse problem?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Implement Queue using Stacks, the converse problem using the opposite pair of structures.
Any "simulate structure A using only structure B's primitives" design problem.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both the two-queue and single-queue approaches achieve the same O(n) push, O(1) pop/top/empty complexity; the single-queue version is simply a more compact implementation of the same rotation idea.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: simulate a LIFO stack using only FIFO queue operations, via rotation.
Core Idea: after every push, rotate the single queue by (size-1) positions so the new element ends up at the front, making pop/top trivial.
Time: O(n) per push, O(1) for pop, top, and empty, for both approaches.
Most Important Observation: rotating the queue right after each push is what converts FIFO order into LIFO order.
Interview Difficulty: a classic, accessible "simulate one structure with another" design problem.
One line memory trick: push, then rotate size-1 times so the new element leads.
